intro: In German journalism a reported claim is carried in the Konjunktiv I, and not just for one clause: after a single introducing verb (erklärte, räumte ein, wies zurück, teilte mit, beteuerte, kündigte an, beklagen) or a source phrase (nach Angaben der Polizei, einer Studie zufolge, wie die Staatsanwaltschaft mitteilte), every following verb of the report stays in the Konjunktiv until the writer speaks in their own voice again. That is the skill this quiz drills — the one that lets you read a newspaper and know who is speaking. Each of the fifteen items is a short press or literary report of two or three sentences with two or three gaps; the infinitives are given in brackets and you type the finite forms in order (sei, habe, werde, könne, müsse, gebe …). Where the Konjunktiv I would look exactly like the indicative – mostly in the plural (sie haben, sie werden, sie können) – you use the Konjunktiv II instead (hätten, würden, könnten); those are the only places where a Konjunktiv II form is accepted. Umlauts count in this quiz: hätten, würden and könnten are the answer, hatten, wurden and konnten are wrong.
tips[0].title: One introducing verb, then the Konjunktiv carries the report
tips[0].text: The report may run for several sentences without another sagte: every finite verb stays in the Konjunktiv I – main clauses, subordinate clauses, questions. A lapse into the indicative in the middle reads as if the paper itself vouched for the claim.
tips[0].trap: English backshifts the tense (was, had been) and stays in the indicative. German does not backshift: the tense of the original stays (ist → sei, war / ist gewesen → sei gewesen, wird → werde); only the mood changes.
tips[0].check.why: The report continues without a new verb of saying, so it stays in the Konjunktiv I. hat or hatte would make it the paper's own claim.

tips[1].title: Forms: third person singular is the workhorse
tips[1].text: Konjunktiv I = infinitive stem + -e: habe, werde, könne, müsse, dürfe, wolle, solle, gebe, lese, fehle, beruhe. sein is irregular: sei / seien. Past = habe / sei + Partizip II (habe gestanden, sei verschwunden); passive past = sei … worden; future = werde + infinitive.
tips[1].check.why: fliehen forms its perfect with sein, and the Konjunktiv I of sein is irregular: er sei, never seie.
tips[2].title: When Konjunktiv I = indicative, switch to Konjunktiv II
tips[2].text: In the plural (and in the first person) most Konjunktiv I forms are identical to the indicative: sie haben, sie werden, sie können. Nobody could see that they are reported, so you take the Konjunktiv II: hätten, würden, könnten. Where Konjunktiv I is distinct (sie seien, er habe, er werde), it stays.
tips[2].trap: Do not overdo it: „er hätte“ where „er habe“ is available sounds as if the writer doubted the claim. Konjunktiv II is the substitute, not the default.
tips[2].check.why: The Konjunktiv I sie können looks like the indicative, so the report switches to the Konjunktiv II könnten. konnten is the plain past.
tips[3].title: Questions and requests in the report
tips[3].text: Reported yes/no questions take ob, W-questions keep their W-word – both with the Konjunktiv (ob die Regierung die Risiken gekannt habe; wer die Verantwortung trage). Reported requests and orders take solle (neutral) or möge (polite, elevated).
tips[3].check.why: A reported yes/no question is introduced by ob, and its verb is in the Konjunktiv: ob … gewusst habe.
remember[0]: One introducing verb, then Konjunktiv I for the whole report; indicative = the paper’s own voice.
remember[1]: sei / seien, habe, werde, könne, müsse, gebe …; hätten / würden / könnten only where Konjunktiv I = indicative.
remember[2]: No tense backshift: the original tense stays, only the mood changes.
table.caption: Journalistic Konjunktiv I and its substitutes
mistakes[0].why: Sustain the Konjunktiv across the whole report.
mistakes[1].why: Plural haben = indicative, so the Konjunktiv II substitute is needed.
mistakes[2].why: habe is distinct from the indicative; Konjunktiv II here suggests the writer doubts him.
hook: Read a German news report and know in every line who is speaking: the source, or the paper itself.
recall.known: From the reported-speech lessons: the Konjunktiv I and its replacement.
recall.today: Keeping it going over a whole paragraph, so every sentence shows whose words they are.
